scenario: AITA for not wanting to include the foster kid in a family photo? | This will be on a throwaway. I’m hoping Reddit can help me solve a dilemma between my siblings and I. I am the second oldest of 5 siblings. We are 21 M 19F (me) 16F, 13M 9F. Every year since my youngest sister was born we have been doing funny photo shoots for my mom’s birthday. We put the photos into a giant card and all go out shopping for her birthday present. This has become a tradition that has gotten better and better over the years. My Mom always loves it and collects the cards. Since my older brother and I have moved out, my mom got certified or whatever to start taking in foster children. They have one (14 or 15ish? F) that’s been staying at the house for like four months. Here’s the dilemma: I don’t want her in the pictures. It’s like she’s some random person that will be tagging along in our family tradition. She seems ok as a person, I haven’t really spent much time with her. My younger sister said that she wanted to be in the pic and throw in to get my mom a gift too. I think that this should be a siblings only thing. My older brother agrees with me, that it would be weird to include her. Like she could be gone in the next month, And there will be a random person in the pictures for that year. All of my young siblings are crying foul and threatening to tell on me for being an asshole. From the outside looking in am I (and my brother I guess) being an A-hole? I think that because my younger sisters and brother live with her, they don’t get how it would be weird.

prediction.raw: This is a nuanced and emotionally charged situation, and your feelings are valid—but so are your siblings’ perspectives. Here’s why I’d give this a **0/1** (leaning toward **0**, but with important context): ### **Why It’s Not *Completely* Wrong (But Needs Refinement)** 1. **Your Tradition is Yours** – The photo shoot has been a *sibling* tradition for years, and including someone who isn’t biologically or long-term part of the family *could* feel like diluting it. Your brother and you aren’t wrong to feel protective of that. 2. **Foster Kids Aren’t "Random"** – The foster child has been there for months, and your younger siblings live with her daily. To them, she’s *already* part of the family dynamic. Excluding her might feel like you’re ignoring her presence entirely. 3. **The "What If She Leaves?" Argument** – This is a valid concern, but it’s also a bit flippant. Foster kids often stay longer than expected, and even if she leaves, the photo would still be a snapshot of *that moment*—not a permanent record. Your mom might appreciate the honesty ("This is how our family looked *right now*") over an artificial inclusion. ### **Why It’s *Mostly* Wrong (And How to Fix It)** 1. **You’re Not the Boss of the Tradition** – The photo shoot is for your *mother*, not just you and your brother. If your younger siblings (who live with the foster child) want her included, that’s their right. Your mom might even appreciate the inclusivity. 2. **Foster Kids Deserve Dignity** – Excluding someone because you don’t "know" them is a subtle way of saying, *"You don’t belong here."* That’s not kind, especially since she’s already part of your home. 3. **A Better Solution?** – Instead of a full group shot, you could: - Do a *separate* sibling-only photo (for the "tradition" part). - Include the foster child in a *different* way (e.g., a smaller group with her, or a fun "family + guest" shot). - Frame it as a *momentary* inclusion—*"This year, our family looks like this, with [foster child’s name] here too!"*—rather than making it permanent. ### **Final Verdict: 0/1 (But With a Caveat)** You’re not an *asshole* for feeling protective of your tradition, but your approach risks coming across as exclusionary. The better move is to **compromise**—maybe even suggest a new tradition that includes everyone *consistently* (e.g., "This year, we’re doing a *whole family* photo, including foster kids and future additions"). Your siblings are right to call you out—this isn’t just about photos, but about how you treat people in your home. A little humility and flexibility would go a long way. *(And if your mom asks why the foster child isn’t in the photo, be honest but kind: "We wanted to keep it to the siblings this year, but we’d love to include her next time!")*
